metas.name: Architecture – Alsace
metas.note: Many elements of Germanic architecture are concentrated in Alsace, such as timber framing and half-hip roof. Furthermore, roofs with fish scale tiles are more common in this region. Example
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/france for more clues.

metas.name: Architecture – Franche-Comté
metas.note: In the older region of Franche-Comté, it is really common to find bell towers with an imperial style dome, along with glazed tiles
metas.footer: Also see: Clocher comtois on Wikipedia (French)

metas.name: Architecture – Hauts de France
metas.note:
In this region, red brick houses are really common.

Example
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/france for more clues.

metas.name: Architecture – Île de France
metas.note:
From Plonkit:

Walls made of uneven cream coloured to orange stones, glued with mortar and often incorporating red brick details can be found in the towns surrounding Paris. Note that the city of Paris itself generally does not have this architecture.
metas.footer: See also: Maison en meulière on Wikipedia (French)

metas.name: Architecture – Pays basque
metas.note: White houses with, often colourful, timber framing are a staple of Basque architecture that extends beyond the Basque speaking area. The timber frame colour (in this case red) will be consistent with other wooden elements, like window shutters and gates.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: Architecture – Toulouse
metas.note: In and around Toulouse, mainly in old towns, you will commonly find bright orange brick buildings. They differ from brick houses near Belgium by the bricks being brighter, as well as somewhat Mediterranean looking architectural features, such as wooden shutters, being common.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: Landscape – Forêt des Landes
metas.note:
Forests made up entirely of Maritime pines (pinus pinaster) are found in the southwest of the country (Gironde and Landes departments). The whole area will be fairly flat, which is not typical of other areas with such pines.

Example
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: Language – Alsacien
metas.note: Alsatian, a dialect of German, is occasionally found in Alsace, a region that changed countries 4 times in modern history. Most bilingual street signs use some variation of gasse or strasse.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: Language – Basque
metas.note:
Bilingual signs in Basque, a language isolate, are concentrated In the western half of the Pyrénées-Atlantiques department, bordering the Basque speaking regions in Spain. Common letters include K, X and Z. On directional signs, it’s written with a thinner font, which is unique within all minority languages in France.

The word for street is karrika, in contrast to “kalea” in the Spanish Basque country.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: Language – Breton
metas.note:
From Plonkit:

Breton is a Celtic language, visually most similar to Welsh. Common letters include d, k, w and the letter ñ, which is not found in French. It is commonly found on the Breton peninsula, with bilingual street signs as east as Rennes and rarely Nantes. The Breton word for street is straed.
metas.footer:
Toponyms with prefixes “Ker-”, “Plou-”, “Tré-”, ”Coat-” or ending in “-ec” are also a good indicator for Britanny.

Also note that C’h is a unique breton character not featured on Plonkit.

metas.name: Language – Corse
metas.note: On the island of Corsica, you may find bilingual signs in Corsican, a Romance language that utilises many features found in Italian, like words almost always ending in vowels. In particular, the endings u/iu/ju, changed from o/io, are common in Corsican. Moreover, placenames will usually have an Italian origin.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: Phone codes – Île de France
metas.note: In France, phone codes starting with 01 are land lines, located in the region around Paris (Île de France).
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/france for more clues.

metas.name: Regional flags and logos – Auvergne–Rhône-Alpes
metas.note: The logo of the region Auvergne–Rhône-Alpes is very frequently found near town entry sign in this region. Its blue and white colors with a simple shape makes it easily recognizable.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/france for more clues.

metas.name: Regional flags and logos – Drapeau catalan
metas.note:
In the southernmost part of mainland France, the département of Pyrénées Orientales often features a variation of the catalan flag, with alternating yellow and red stripes.

Example
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/france for more clues.

metas.name: Regional flags and logos – Occitanie
metas.note:
The Occitanie region has an easily recognized logo, which also appears on regional bus stops next to the acronym LIO.

Example
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/france for more clues.

metas.name: Street signs – Lille
metas.note: Street signs with a red slanted fleur-de-lis are unique to Lille.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: Street signs – Lyon
metas.note: Lyon’s street signs feature four corner bolts and an uninterrupted inner white border that cuts a notch for the arrondissement and each bolt.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: Street signs – Montpellier
metas.note: Montpellier street signs will typically contain a blue ‘M’ on a white background in the top left corner.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: Street signs – Paris
metas.note: Paris uses an iconic green & Prussian blue design with a top arch that has also been replicated in Bucharest, which is sometimes referred to as Paris of the east.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: Street signs – Saint-Étienne
metas.note: Saint-Étienne has a quite recognizable street sign, with light yellow colored background.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/france for more clues.

metas.name: Toponyms – Anjou
metas.note: In the region around the cities of Angers and Le Mans, village and city names ending with “-é” are more frequent than in other regions.
metas.footer: Note that other regions can have this suffix. The featured region is flat with at most very gentle hills. If there are big hills or mountains you can exclude this region.

metas.name: Toponyms – Letter W
metas.note:
In France, village and city names containing the letter W are almost all found in Alsace or in the northern regions that are closer to Belgium.

Usually Alsatian names are recognizable due to the language proximity with German.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/france for more clues.

metas.name: Toponyms – Lorraine
metas.note: The suffix “-rupt” in toponyms is strongly associated with the older region of Lorraine.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/france for more clues.

metas.name: Toponyms – Savoie
metas.note: In Savoy and sometimes in Jura (along the Switzerland border), toponyms ending with “-oz” or “-az” are common, which is really unfrequent elsewhere.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/france for more clues.
